newsitem.title: USA: Irate shareholders blast Northeast chief at meeting.
newsitem.headline: Irate shareholders blast Northeast chief at meeting.

text.p: Angry shareholders confronted Northeast Utilities Chairman, President and Chief Executive Bernard Fox on Tuesday over the company's prolonged nuclear crisis and suspension of its dividend.
Some of the 800 shareholders who attended the troubled utility's annual meeting blasted Fox over the company's plummeting stock price and nuclear outage-related costs.
They were also displeased when Chief Financial Officer John Forsgren said the company will not consider restoring its quarterly dividend until the second quarter of 1998 at the earliest.

Fox, 54, will retire later this year after the company names a successor. He told shareholders that Northeast was actively searching for a new chief executive and was considering candidates from inside and outside the electric industry.
"My expectation is that a new chief executive will be named in the late third quarter or early fourth quarter, at which time I will retire," Fox said.

Fox, who has worked at Northeast for 33 years, will be paid $800,000 over the next two years to serve as a consultant after he retires, according to company documents. He will also earn a pension of $400,000 a year.
Shareholder Sherman London of Southbury, Conn., said during a question-and-answer session: "I vigorously protest the unconscionable payments to Mr. Fox as a consultant over the next two years."

London said it was under Fox's leadership that the company collapsed. Northeast's three Millstone nuclear power plants in Waterford, Conn., have been closed for safety reasons since March 1996. The utility has projected its nuclear outage-related costs at $990 million through 1998.

Northeast Nuclear Chief Executive Bruce Kenyon reiterated to shareholders Tuesday that the company expects to have the three Millstone plants back on line by early next year, pending approval by federal regulators.

Another shareholder, Marvin Klein of Wilton, Conn., told Fox, "You were hired to protect retired persons. I don't see why you should get any kind of pension at all, because you have screwed up this company."
Fox thanked the shareholders for their comments and said the company was striving mightily to restore shareholder value.
Kenyon told reporters after the meeting that the restoration of the Millstone plants would help give Northeast a financial shot in the arm.

"That will create revenue for the company that doesn't exist today, and that will be a very important step not only towards re-establishing the dividend but establishing investor confidence in the company, which should allow significant recovery of stock price," Kenyon said.
Northeast shares declined in 1996 from $25.25 to $9.50. The stock was unchanged at $9.125 in consolidated Tuesday afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Berlin, Conn.-based Northeast serves 1.7 million customers in Connecticut, New Hampshire and western Massachusetts.
